name: nim-regex (nitely/regex)
workload: Find-all of email/URI/IPv4 regex patterns over a concatenated text corpus (learnxinyminutes-docs), measured on a MacBook Pro 16-inch 2019 (2.4GHz i9); benchmark also includes C PCRE2, Rust regex crate, and C++ STL std::regex in the same harness
claimed_speedup: Default-settings run: nim-regex totals 36.09ms vs C PCRE2's 251.37ms (~7.0x faster) and vs C++ STL std::regex's 1023.49ms (~28x faster); also ~1.6x faster than default Rust regex (57.63ms). In the 'optimized' run, nim-regex totals 34.15ms, still ~2.6x faster than optimized PCRE2 (87.87ms) and ~30x faster than C++ STL (1021.10ms), but optimized Rust regex (27.94ms) edges out nim-regex by ~1.2x on that run.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 1.4.4 (nimble package 'regex'); comparison harness: gcc 7.5.0 & PCRE2 10.36-2 (C), rustc 1.51.0 & regex 1.4.5 (Rust), g++ 7.5.0 (C++ STL), run via Docker image mariomka/regex-benchmark:1.6
hardware: MacBook Pro 16-inch 2019, 2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, 32 GB 2667 MHz DDR4, macOS Big Sur 11.2.3
tradeoffs: Nim-only (not usable from C/C++ without FFI wrapping); guarantees linear-time matching (no catastrophic backtracking) via a DFA/NFA hybrid, PCRE-like syntax but with Unicode level-1 support only; benchmark corpus (concatenated tutorial docs) may not represent all real workloads.
caveats: This is a third-party cross-language shootout (mariomka/regex-benchmark), not the nim-regex project's own benchmark, but it is a well-known, reproducible, versioned suite with stated compiler/flags/hardware, so it qualifies for tier A. The lead over PCRE2 shrinks a lot once PCRE2 is 'optimized' (its default-settings run under-configures PCRE2), and in that optimized run Rust's regex crate (also a named baseline) actually narrowly beats nim-regex on total time, so the 'faster than Rust regex' claim only holds in the default-settings table, not the optimized one.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "regex-benchmark" --sort stars --limit 20 -> mariomka/regex-benchmark README, cross-referenced nim/benchmark_regex.nim source (imports pkg/regex) to identify 'Nim Regex' as nitely/nim-regex

name: SafeRE
workload: JMH microbenchmarks: 150-row real-world matrix (25 patterns x match/no-match x 1K/10K/100K input sizes), plus 8 'Core' and 8 'Application' workloads, run against java.util.regex (JDK), RE2/J, RE2-FFM (Java FFM binding to native C++ RE2), native C++ RE2, PCRE2 JIT, Go regexp, Rust regex crate, and .NET's non-backtracking engine.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 2.22x faster than JDK java.util.regex on the 150-row real-world matrix (1.88x after removing 2 pathological backtracking rows), but 22% slower than JDK on the smaller 'Core' set and 7% slower on 'Application'. Also 12.5x faster than RE2/J and 3.06x faster than RE2-FFM on the real-world matrix. However, against the three canonical native baselines it directly benchmarked: SafeRE is 13% slower than native C++ RE2, takes 2.47x as long as PCRE2 JIT, and takes 2.03x as long as Rust's regex crate on the same 150-row matrix (though 1.32x faster than native RE2 on the smaller 'Core' subset).
compiler_and_flags: Java: OpenJDK 26.0.2+10-55 targeting Java 21, JMH 1.37 (2 forks, 2 warmup iters x500ms, 5 measurement iters x500ms); C++: g++ 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG, RE2 snapshot 2025-11-05; PCRE2 10.47 with JIT enabled; Go 1.26.1 linux/amd64; Rust rustc 1.97.1 with regex 1.13.1; .NET SDK 10.0.110
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K, 8 cores/16 threads, 3.6 GHz base, 16 GiB RAM under WSL2, Ubuntu 24.04 on Windows 11 host, Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2
tradeoffs: 71.2x slower to compile a pattern than the JDK (11.7x slower than RE2/J), and retains substantially more memory per compiled pattern, in exchange for guaranteed linear-time matching with no catastrophic-backtracking risk (e.g. 0.089us vs the JDK's 17,079us on an adversarial pattern). Cross-runtime ratios mix FFI/marshalling overhead with engine cost, so they are not pure same-runtime comparisons.
caveats: SafeRE is a from-scratch Java port of RE2's design (not a GitHub fork), so is_fork_of is null even though it is explicitly 'based on RE2'. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION because the LICENSE file is a compound notice, but the file text states both RE2 and RE2/J (and by extension this port) are BSD-3-Clause. Critically, on the primary 150-row real-world matrix, SafeRE is NOT faster than any of the three named baselines it tested that are on our incumbent list (RE2, PCRE2, Rust regex) -- it is slower than all three there; its clear win is only over java.util.regex, which is a widely used incumbent but not one of PCRE2/RE2/std::regex/Rust regex. This is an unusually rigorous, self-critical benchmark report (authors explicitly flag their own losses), which raises confidence in the numbers despite the mixed result.

name: nanoregex
workload: Regex search over a 142 KB Zig source file, 200 iterations, 8 patterns (literal, literal-prefix, alternation, \d+, [a-z]+, IPv4-like, etc.), comparing nanoregex (ReleaseFast build) against Python's re module and against its own predecessor zig-regex 0.1.1 on a catastrophic-backtracking pattern.
claimed_speedup: 1.65x-2.8x faster than Python re on 7 of 8 non-anchored patterns tested (1 pattern was 1.5x slower than Python); separately, ~5000x faster than the predecessor library zig-regex 0.1.1 on a pattern that triggers catastrophic backtracking (43 seconds -> 8 milliseconds), and reduced a real zigrepper CLI query from 43s to 0.43s end-to-end.
tradeoffs: Pure Zig, no FFI/dependencies; dispatches between a literal memmem fast path, a lazy subset-construction DFA (byte-minterm compressed), and a Pike-VM fallback for correctness. Does not yet support lookaround, named groups, in-pattern backreferences, or Unicode property classes -- those fall back or diverge from a richer engine.
caveats: First-party README benchmark with no CPU model stated, so capped at tier C per the rubric even though build flags are given. The headline ~5000x figure is versus zig-regex 0.1.1, a niche predecessor library that is not one of the four named category baselines (PCRE2/RE2/std::regex/Rust regex) and not a widely-used incumbent, so that number should be discounted; the more relevant comparison is the 1.65x-2.8x win over Python's re module, which is a widely used incumbent but not on the named-baseline list. Very small/new project (2 stars), included per the DO-NOT-EXCLUDE-ON-SIZE rule.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "zig regex" --sort stars --limit 15 -> justrach/nanoregex README

name: re2jit
workload: Repo-bundled perf tests: a small Markdown-to-HTML converter using two regexes with capture groups (make test/32-markdownish), and a tokenizer for the 'dg' language whose pattern relies on a Unicode class equivalent to \w (make test/30-long), comparing re2jit's JIT-compiled Thompson-NFA-to-x86-64 approach against google/re2 directly.
claimed_speedup: Exactly as fast as RE2 for simple unanchored search with discarded groups (falls back to RE2's own DFA); 20-30% faster than RE2 when capture-group boundaries must be reported; up to 100x faster than RE2 on patterns using full Unicode character classes (e.g. \pL), because re2jit matches a whole code point via a 2-stage lookup table instead of RE2's enumerated-alternation expansion.
tradeoffs: x86-64 only (hand-written asm64 DSL that JIT-compiles into mmapped executable memory); does not implement \b/\B word boundaries at all; reserves Unicode plane-15 private-use code points internally. Backreferences are supported with a guaranteed-linear-time fast path when no backreferenced group is repeated, exponential otherwise (same as general backreference semantics).
caveats: First-party claim in the README with no CPU model, compiler, or exact timing numbers given (only percentage/multiplier ranges and 'run this make target yourself'), so capped at tier C. Project is abandoned since 2016 (>3 years, tagged per DO-NOT-EXCLUDE rules rather than skipped) and the author's own README notes that 'new versions of re2 have significantly improved Unicode charclass performance,' meaning the up-to-100x figure is very likely stale and would be much smaller against current RE2.

name: re2c (Go backend / re2go)
baseline: PCRE (via go-pcre cgo binding; not confirmed to be PCRE2)
workload: Short-regex matching (email/URI/IPv4 patterns) over a text corpus, comparing 12 Go-ecosystem regex options -- including re2c's Go code-generation backend ('re2go'), a PCRE cgo binding, RE2 cgo/WASM bindings, Hyperscan cgo binding, and Go's native regexp -- on Linux with an Intel i7-8550U.
claimed_speedup: re2go totals 45.85ms vs the PCRE cgo binding's 53.16ms on the same corpus (~1.16x faster, derived from page data: 53.16/45.85). Both are reported relative to Go's native regexp baseline as 18.65x and 16.08x respectively. re2go is, however, slower than the RE2 cgo binding (29.07ms) and the Hyperscan cgo binding (50.55ms is actually slower than re2go, so re2go beats Hyperscan here too, ~1.10x, though Hyperscan already appears on the KNOWN_LIST).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U, 16 GB RAM, Linux
license: Public Domain (dedication, not a formal OSI license)
stars_or_usage: 1.31k stars (re2c project); used in production by PHP and Ninja per the benchmark author
tradeoffs: re2c/re2go is a compile-time regex-to-code compiler (like a lexer generator), not a runtime-compiled regex API -- patterns must be known and compiled into Go source ahead of time, and its syntax is Flex-like rather than fully Go/PCRE-compatible, so it is not a drop-in replacement.
caveats: Margin over the PCRE binding is thin (~16%) and derived by us from the page's per-column totals rather than stated directly as a ratio versus PCRE specifically. The go-pcre package name suggests classic PCRE1 rather than PCRE2, which was not confirmed, so baseline_in_list is set to false; this benchmark used a synthetic short-text corpus (learnxinyminutes concatenation) that the benchmark's own author says may not be representative, and no compiler flags for the C/CGO libraries were stated, so capped at tier C rather than B.
